Your values are kind of like your inner cheerleader. They motivate you to do the things you care about. Your values represent what you think is most important in life. So let's take a closer look at that inner cheerleader. Now this is important. Why you ask? Because your values help shape all of your financial decisions. What material things are important to you? Learn

Build the idea

Three different clues

An is an activity that attracts your attention. A skill is something you can do, and stronger evidence comes from a specific task and result. A work value is a condition or purpose you care about, such as variety, stability, helping others, working outdoors, or flexible hours. Liking drawing does not prove that Jordan enjoys client deadlines; organizing a group does not prove a particular occupation is the only match.

Required checkpoint

Use Explore Your Occupational Options now

Open Explore Your Occupational Options ↗

Not checked yet

Move from labels to examples

Instead of writing ‘good communicator,’ name what you did: explained a complex idea to a younger student, checked whether they understood, and changed your example. That evidence can transfer to many roles. Ask what parts of the experience gave you energy and what was difficult. An interest inventory can suggest possibilities, but its results are questions to investigate, not instructions about your future.

Test a first hypothesis

Make a short list of possible roles, including one outside your first idea. For each, compare actual day-to-day tasks, training, work conditions, and location. A provisional career hypothesis might say, ‘I want to explore jobs that combine visual problem solving with explaining ideas.’ It remains open to change after you read profiles, meet course requirements, or try a simulated task.

Check the quality of your evidence

A useful evidence note has a context, an action, and an observable result. “I organized people well” is difficult to test; “I asked each group member what they could finish, put the tasks on a shared checklist, and noticed one deadline was at risk” gives a reader something concrete. Then add a boundary: the event involved classmates and one deadline, so it does not prove the learner will enjoy managing a large team. Strong reflection includes what was hard and what support helped, not only praise.

Look for patterns without turning them into labels

One example can suggest a question; several examples across different settings can suggest a pattern. If someone enjoys explaining a science demonstration and helping a younger cousin with a game, the shared clue may be adapting explanations, not “must become a teacher.” Ask what part of each task was satisfying, what conditions mattered, and whether the skill appeared again. A quiet learner can show communication through careful writing or listening; evidence does not need to look like public speaking. Use the pattern to choose a next experiment, such as comparing two roles’ daily tasks.

Explore Your Occupational Options cannot establish that graphic design fits Jordan or will lead to a job. Check current occupation profiles and local postings for duties, conditions, and entry routes.

Learn

Build the idea

Start with work, not a title

Career clusters group related work, but a broad label can hide major differences. An occupation profile can describe main duties, conditions, education, certifications, skills, and typical pay. Read the daily activities first: what would you spend a Tuesday doing? Then identify the entry requirement and whether it is legally required, commonly preferred, or one of several routes. The distinction affects the time and cost of a plan.

Required checkpoint

Check Graphic Designer — alis: duties and conditions

Locate one daily duty and one working condition. Keep those as separate evidence; a duty describes the work, while a condition describes where or when it happens.

Open Graphic Designer — alis ↗

Not checked yet

Compare sources with dates

A provincial profile summarizes an occupation across workplaces; a job posting describes one employer’s current opening. The two can differ without either being wrong. Record the profile’s source, region, and update date. A wage range does not promise that a new worker will receive the midpoint. A posting that asks for experience may be one route rather than the only route into the occupation.

Required checkpoint

Check Graphic Designer — alis: page details

Record the page title, Alberta scope, page or section date, and the day you accessed it. Those details let another reader find the same evidence.

Open Graphic Designer — alis ↗

Not checked yet

Investigate the gaps

Use a profile to draft questions. Does the work require travel or shift work? Is a licence needed in Alberta? Does training need to be renewed? What related roles use the same skills? Compare at least two roles and identify what you cannot settle from the profile alone. Later, you can use program pages and current postings to test the picture.

Required checkpoint

Check Graphic Designer — alis: what it cannot confirm

Choose one preparation statement and decide what another current source must confirm, such as a regulator, program provider, or employer.

Open Graphic Designer — alis ↗

Not checked yet

Separate typical work from entry requirements

Profiles often combine tasks that occur frequently with requirements that apply only to some employers or specialties. Mark each statement as “typical task,” “legal or credential requirement,” “common preference,” or “one posting’s condition.” If the profile says a credential is required for a regulated occupation, verify that claim on the relevant Alberta regulator’s current page. If one employer prefers experience, that does not automatically make it a universal entry rule. A profile helps you build a research trail; it cannot replace checking the current rules attached to a specific role.

Use source disagreement as a question

When two profiles disagree, compare the occupation name and code, region, update date, and the question each source answers. A national page might summarize a broad occupation, while an Alberta employer lists a narrow specialty. Do not average the statements or choose the one that sounds more encouraging. Record the conflict and identify a source closer to the decision, such as an official regulator for licensing or the program provider for admissions. If no authoritative answer appears, write “not yet verified” and ask an advisor before paying for training.

Quick tip: What Graphic Designer — alis cannot answer

Graphic Designer — alis summarizes work across Alberta settings. It cannot confirm a local opening, one employer’s expectations, admission, or Jordan’s personal fit.

Number two, make good choices. Follow our super handy decision making guide. This will help you with any decision, but will also help you make the best career choice for you. Start by defining the decision you have to make. In this case, what career to plan for, then establish your criteria. That's what's important to you in a job. FINLIT 101 excerpt, used with permission. The lesson below teaches the idea in text.

Learn

Build the idea

Work backward from the destination

Start with the exact role and confirm its real entry requirements. Some roles require a regulated credential; others accept different combinations of courses, work experience, portfolios, certificates or degrees. A college program, apprenticeship, direct employment and entrepreneurial route can lead to related work but not necessarily the same licence. Check the current program and regulator pages rather than relying on a friend’s memory.

Required checkpoint

Use Explore School and Program Options now

Use the alis page to identify a route or program detail learners should compare, such as entry information or a next research step; distinguish it from a confirmed admission rule.

Open Explore School and Program Options ↗

Not checked yet

Calculate the whole route

Tuition is only one cost. Include tools, fees, transport, housing, time without full earnings, and any paid training. Compare what is known and label uncertain estimates. For example, a $2,000 fee with $1,200 travel costs is $3,200 in direct costs; it says nothing yet about income during the program. A lower up-front cost may still take longer, and a faster route may be less flexible if the learner later changes goals.

Keep alternatives live

Make a primary route and a backup route. Record prerequisites to verify, a question for a school counsellor or program advisor, and a date to revisit the choice. A route map is useful when it can change with new evidence. It should not lock a student into a plan based on invented earnings or an unverified admission rule.

Compare more than the first payment

A route comparison should identify when each cost occurs and which items are estimates. Up-front tuition, required equipment, application fees, transportation, housing, and time away from paid work can affect different learners differently. Keep one-time and recurring costs separate; a $400 tool purchase and $40 monthly travel cost cannot be compared by simply adding them without choosing a time period. Identify scholarships or paid training only when a current, eligible source supports them. If financing is needed, make borrowing a separate decision with its own total-cost and repayment analysis.

Check whether the routes reach the same destination

Two programs may share a subject but lead to different credentials or scopes of practice. Trace the chain: program completion, any exam or supervised hours, registration or licence, then the actual job title. Ask the regulator or program provider which parts are mandatory, whether prior learning counts, and what happens if a learner pauses. Draw a decision point where evidence could change the plan. This protects a student from comparing one route’s introductory certificate with another route’s full as if they were interchangeable.

Read the lesson’s written equivalent

A headline is a clue, not a job offer. Start with the question you are actually trying to answer. Sam wants an entry-level job within travelling distance of home.

Document A reports a provincial median of twenty-eight dollars an hour. Median means the middle observation in an ordered set. It does not mean every worker earns that amount. The data include different experience levels, so Sam cannot treat the median as a starting wage.

Document B lists a local assistant job at nineteen dollars an hour. That is useful for this particular opening, but it does not describe the entire occupation. It may also be a different role from the occupation in Document A.

Now compare the dates. The report was published in 2026, but its wage observations are from 2024. A recent publication date does not automatically make every number current.

A careful conclusion is: I have evidence worth investigating, but not a guaranteed job or starting salary. Sam's next step is to check the role, entry requirements and travel, then compare another relevant source.

Learn

Build the idea

Name what was measured

Labour-market sources may report employment, vacancies, wages, projections, or employer expectations. Those are different measures. A provincial can describe a multi-year pattern while a job search shows advertised openings on one day. Neither directly predicts whether Noor will be hired after training. Write the measure, occupation definition, region, date, and source next to every figure so a reader can judge its relevance.

Compare like with like

A for experienced workers should not be presented as a starting wage. A province-wide shortage does not prove that jobs are available in one town. Before comparing two reports, check whether they cover the same occupation code, geography and time period. A small number of current postings may reflect a seasonal hiring cycle, an employer that recruits another way, or a genuinely limited local market.

Use uncertainty to plan

The right result is usually a conditional plan. Noor can explore nearby related roles, check training and travel costs, look for recent postings over time, and ask what work is available locally. If moving is a possible option, it belongs alongside housing, support and lifestyle costs. Record what evidence would change the plan instead of labelling a pathway safe or unsafe from one graph.

Read the axis before the trend

Before using a table, chart, or headline, record its title, unit or measure, category, time window, geographic coverage, and publication date. A forecast, an employment count, a wage range, and a one-day vacancy search answer different questions. Check whether the categories use matching definitions and whether the source describes a current observation or a future model. Copy the source name and retrieval date into your notes so the claim can be checked later.

Triangulate without pretending to predict

A second source is useful when it adds a different kind of evidence: current local postings, a provincial outlook, or an occupational profile. More sources do not automatically mean stronger evidence if all repeat the same old estimate. If one report suggests growth and current local postings are scarce, write both findings and consider season, region, commute, job title, and the date each was observed. Learn

Build the idea

Work from current requirements

A high-school plan connects a possible destination to courses and experiences available now. Start with the current admission or entry page for each . Record required courses separately from recommended preparation. Note grade thresholds and deadlines only when a current source states them, because they may change. Ask the school to confirm sequencing, availability and graduation requirements rather than assuming that a program page describes your timetable.

Not checked yet

Find the shared steps

Two routes often share foundational courses and skills. Place those common steps first, then mark a decision point where a specialized course or application is needed. If one course has a , draw the chain: prerequisite, later course, program requirement. A chain reveals why delaying a course may close an option temporarily and where a summer, online or alternate route might exist if the school confirms it.

Make revision part of the plan

Put a date and trigger on each checkpoint. A new interest, changed grade, updated program requirement or transport issue can justify revision. A useful backup route is a researched pathway, not ‘do something else.’ Keep a note of who can verify an uncertainty. This protects students from treating an early plan as an unchangeable promise.

Trace prerequisites as a sequence

A prerequisite is not only a course name; it is a dependency that affects when a later option can be taken. Draw a simple chain with the source and school confirmation beside each step. If a course is unavailable in a planned term, ask about the next offering, approved equivalent, or alternate route before deleting a career goal. Keep graduation requirements distinct from a specific college admission requirement. A school timetable and a university program page answer different questions, and both may need current confirmation.

Build a checkpoint around a decision

Each route can have a “continue, revise, or investigate” point. For example, after reviewing the official admission page and meeting a counsellor, the learner can confirm the course sequence or identify an unresolved conflict. Record the date, evidence checked, and who can verify the next uncertainty. Avoid turning a grade threshold into a personal worth judgement: a result is information for choosing support or a different sequence. A backup route is strongest when it shares useful preparation and has been researched, not when it is simply a vague fallback.

why you'd be a good person to hire. When it comes to resumes, there is no one standard formatter template to use, though there are many templates available online if you need help starting out. Most resumes do, however, contain certain standard sections and information. It's always good to include a cover letter along with your resume. Read the written record

Before you continue: Keep Three Rights of Workers open. The required checkpoint in the teaching tells you when to return to it.

Learn

Build the idea

A hazard is a source of harm

A is not the same as an injury that has already happened. The unlabelled liquid creates uncertainty about exposure; the ventilation condition may increase risk. Before starting, identify what could go wrong, who could be affected and what information is missing. A worker should receive the information, instruction, training and supervision needed for the task. An instruction to ‘be careful’ does not identify the substance or safe procedure.

Required checkpoint

Open Three Rights of Workers ↗

Not checked yet

Use the three rights

Canadian occupational health and safety guidance describes the rights to know about hazards, participate in health and safety decisions, and refuse work that may endanger someone. The right to know supports requesting the label, safety information and training before use. Participation includes reporting the concern and suggesting a safer method. If dangerous conditions remain, the worker should follow the applicable refusal process; the exact procedure belongs to the jurisdiction and workplace.

Control the risk and document

Pause the task, keep others away from the uncertain exposure if safe to do so, and ask the supervisor for guidance and the correct procedure. Do not test an unknown chemical by smelling it or mixing it with another product. Record the concern through the workplace process and follow up. If an immediate serious danger exists, move to safety and use the emergency procedure. The lesson case is fictional; a real worker should use current Alberta guidance and workplace training.

Choose a control that removes or reduces exposure

Risk control is strongest when it eliminates the hazard or separates people from it, rather than depending only on reminders to be careful. For the unknown cleaner in the case, a learner should not touch, smell, mix, or pour it. Keep people away if safe, report it, and wait for someone trained to identify and handle it. A glove or mask is not a substitute for knowing what the substance is and whether that equipment is appropriate.

Refusal is a process, not a dare

The right to refuse dangerous work is not an invitation to take risks or to confront someone alone. Tell the supervisor promptly, explain the specific hazard, and follow the current workplace and Alberta OHS process. The supervisor may investigate and take corrective action; the worker should not resume until the concern is addressed through the process. If danger is immediate, leave the danger area and follow emergency directions. The exact legal process and any exceptions must be checked against current official guidance. Pause and decide: Before Devin acts: name the hazard, the missing information, and the safest next step.

Read the lesson’s written equivalent

Slide 1: The first shift

A request is not the same as safe information. UNLABELLED LIQUID; POOR VENTILATION; SUPERVISOR BUSY. What is unknown?

A first shift is a time to ask, not guess. Devin is asked to use a cleaning liquid beside a storage area with poor ventilation. There is no readable label, and the supervisor is helping another worker. A coworker says, “It is probably the usual cleaner.” That description is not enough to identify the substance or its safe use. Pause the task. We will separate what Devin observed from what still needs confirmation.

Slide 2: Name the hazard and the gap

Describe evidence before deciding what the substance is. OBSERVED: container has no readable label; CONDITION: air feels stale; ventilation uncertain; UNKNOWN: contents, exposure risk, required controls. Observed fact ≠ confirmed identity

A hazard is a source or condition that could cause harm. Here, the unlabeled container creates uncertainty; the ventilation condition may affect exposure. Devin should not infer the chemical from its colour, smell, or a coworker’s guess. The missing information includes the product identity, its instructions, possible exposure routes, and the site procedure. This is a case about a missing safety control, not about diagnosing a chemical or deciding whether a law was broken.

Slide 3: Use the three worker rights

Know • Participate • Refuse dangerous work KNOW: ask for hazard information and training; PARTICIPATE: report the concern and suggest a control; REFUSE: follow the applicable process if danger remains. Rights guide a safe process

Canadian workplace safety guidance describes three worker rights: to know about hazards, to participate in health and safety decisions, and to refuse work that may endanger someone. Devin can request the product label, the relevant safety information, instruction, and supervision. Devin can report the concern and take part in choosing a safer method. If the hazard remains, the worker follows the applicable refusal process; it is not a dare or an invitation to confront someone alone. Details belong to the current Alberta process and workplace.

Slide 4: Choose an immediate control

Reduce exposure before collecting more detail. 1 STOP the task; 2 KEEP CLEAR if safe; 3 TELL the supervisor; 4 WAIT for trained direction. Never smell • mix • pour • test

The safe immediate move is to stop before handling the container. If it is safe, Devin should keep other people away from the area and alert the supervisor or designated trained person. Devin should not smell the liquid, mix it with another cleaner, pour it down a drain, or carry it to find a label. Those actions can create exposure or a reaction. If there is immediate serious danger, move to safety and follow the site emergency procedure.

Slide 5: Pause: make the decision

Name the hazard, missing evidence, and next safe action. What is observed?; What must be confirmed?; What should Devin do now?. Pause the video and write a 1–2 sentence response.

Before Devin acts: name the hazard, the missing information, and the safest next step. Pause here and decide.

Slide 6: Worked response and follow-up

State facts, ask for controls, and close the loop. DO NOT handle the unknown liquid; Ask for identity, information, training, and procedure; Record the concern through the site process. A good response is specific—not dramatic.

A strong response says: the container has no readable label, ventilation is uncertain, and Devin has not received the safe procedure. Devin pauses, keeps clear if safe, alerts the supervisor, and asks for the identity, hazard information, training, and approved control before using it. The misconception is that a familiar-looking product or coworker’s confidence makes handling safe. It does not. After the hazard is addressed, Devin records the outcome and follows up. For an actual workplace, check current Alberta guidance and site instructions; this example does not decide a legal case. Before closing, Devin checks who will identify the liquid and what training is needed before anyone resumes the task. If no trained person is available, the area remains controlled and the concern is escalated through the site process. The follow-up is not “clean it up later”; it is to confirm that a responsible person has identified the product, selected controls, and explained how to work safely. This makes the handoff concrete and prevents the unknown hazard from becoming the next shift’s problem.

Learn

Build the idea

Responsibilities are shared

A safe workplace requires more than one person following rules. Employers must provide systems, information and supervision required by applicable law; workers follow safe procedures, use provided protection correctly and report hazards. Saying ‘everyone is responsible’ does not mean a new worker must solve a hazardous system alone. In the case, the worker can stop a task they cannot do safely and ask how the inspection should be completed.

Required checkpoint

Make the concern specific

A useful report names the task, observed condition, time and possible consequence. ‘The machine is dangerous’ is less actionable than ‘the guard was loose during the 4 p.m. closing check; I stopped using it and told the shift lead.’ Keep facts separate from assumptions about someone’s motives. Follow the workplace process and keep an appropriate record, without sharing private worker information publicly.

Escalate with purpose

If the first conversation does not resolve a concern, use the next workplace contact or current Alberta occupational health and safety guidance. For wage or scheduling matters, the relevant employment-standards route may differ from a safety concern. Identify the issue before selecting an agency or complaint path. Asking a trusted adult, union representative where applicable, or school contact for help can support a young worker.

Choose the right reporting route for the issue

A workplace can involve several distinct concerns: an immediate hazard, unpaid wages, schedule limits, harassment, or unsafe equipment. Start by naming the issue and its urgency. A safety concern belongs in the workplace OHS reporting process and may involve Alberta OHS guidance; a pay question may involve the employer’s payroll records and Employment Standards. Some situations need more than one route. Avoid sending a complaint to an agency that has no mandate for that issue, and seek a trusted adult’s help when uncertain.

Close the loop after reporting

A report is more useful when it states what action is requested and how the worker will know whether the risk was addressed. For example, “Please confirm the guard is secured and show me the inspection procedure before I use the saw again.” Note the response and any change to the equipment or instruction. If the hazard persists, follow the escalation path rather than treating silence as resolution. Do not photograph coworkers or publish allegations online; preserve relevant records privately and use the workplace’s appropriate channels. Keep the report factual and limited to people who need to respond. A clear record helps identify whether a control changed and prevents the same hazard from being passed to the next shift.

Before you continue: Keep Learn What Is on Your Pay Stub open. The required checkpoint in the teaching tells you when to return to it.

Watch and notice

Why gross and net pay differ

Listen for the difference between gross earnings and take-home pay. Then use Mika’s fictional statement to calculate each amount and explain the listed deductions.

Read the draft transcript

Visuals: a drawn pay slip separates gross pay and deductions and highlights income tax. The on-screen document is illustrative; use the fully labelled HTML pay statement below for the lesson arithmetic.

Often there can be a bit of shock when you look at your paycheck and see the gross pay amount, the amount before deductions, compared to the net pay amount, the amount of money you actually get. What is all that money that is being subtracted? Let's dig into paycheck deductions a little more so we can get a better understanding of what those amounts that are being deducted actually are. First, we have income tax. By law, an employer must deduct the amount of federal and provincial income tax you're likely to over the year and submit it to the government on your behalf. Taxes go towards things like roads, schools, parks and hospitals. You may also see Canada Pension Plan or CPP.

FINLIT 101 excerpt, used with permission. The lesson below teaches the idea in text.

Learn

Build the idea

Understand the evidence

A pay stub is a record of how an employer calculated one pay period. Begin with the period dates and hours, then find the rate and gross earnings. is the amount before deductions. For hourly work, regular hours multiplied by the hourly rate gives regular earnings; overtime, holiday pay, tips, or other items may appear separately when applicable. A salaried worker may instead see a salary amount apportioned by pay period. Do not multiply an annual salary by the number of weeks unless the period and pay arrangement support that calculation. First ask, “What work and time does this statement cover?” A mismatch between expected and recorded hours is a question to investigate, not proof of wrongdoing. Keep this course example fictional: it teaches how to read a statement, not what any particular worker should receive.

Required checkpoint

Use Learn What Is on Your Pay Stub now

Use the guide to locate a pay-statement line learners should compare with hours worked, and distinguish that explanation from the lesson’s fictional arithmetic.

Open Learn What Is on Your Pay Stub ↗

Not checked yet

Make the calculation or comparison

Next, classify each subtraction rather than treating every as the same thing. A statement may show income-tax withholding, statutory contributions, benefit-plan premiums, or an employee-authorized amount. The labels and whether they apply depend on current law, eligibility, employer arrangements, and the worker’s situation. This lesson will not teach fixed deduction rates because those can change and depend on details. For the arithmetic, add the listed deductions and subtract that total from gross pay: = gross pay − total deductions. Net pay is the deposit amount only when the statement has no other payment method or adjustment. Check whether a line is a deduction from this cheque or an employer-paid contribution shown for information. Never infer from a label alone that the amount is correct; compare the pay period, hours, agreement, and current official guidance, then ask an appropriate payroll contact if a real discrepancy remains.

Use the result carefully

Use a deliberate reading sequence: (1) verify the pay-period dates, (2) calculate gross earnings from the supplied hours and rate, (3) compare that result to the gross line, (4) add the listed deductions, (5) subtract and compare with net pay, and (6) explain one uncertainty. This method is useful because a correct total can still hide an incorrect hour count, while an unusual net amount can result from a legitimate deduction or a changed pay period. When comparing two jobs, compare more than hourly wage: hours available, predictable scheduling, paid time, benefits, travel, and safety also affect the value of work. FINLIT’s paycheque material introduces gross and net pay and common deduction categories; the examples here use invented values and deliberately avoid its dated CPP figures or treating every listed category as universal. A readable statement plus the calculation is the lesson; a video is a preview, not a substitute for examining the evidence.

Quick tip: What Learn What Is on Your Pay Stub cannot answer

The decision

Check gross earnings

Watch the reasoning

  1. Begin with the pay period and payment date. Then check hours × rate against gross earnings before looking at deductions.
  2. Group deductions by label and add them. Net pay should equal gross earnings minus deductions in this simplified fictional record. Year-to-date amounts are cumulative and should not be subtracted again.
  3. Finally compare the hours with the supplied time record. If the arithmetic is correct but the hours differ, the next action is to ask payroll for a review with the record attached.

Watch a worked decision

Read Mika’s fictional pay stub

Watch Mika’s fictional pay statement being read and reconciled. Pause to calculate gross pay and deductions before the answer appears.

Pause and decide: Calculate gross pay and total deductions. What does a match establish—and what does it not prove?

Read the narrated and visual transcript

Slide 1: A smaller deposit

Start by finding the period—not by guessing at an error. Pay period • May 1–14; 12.5 regular hours × $18.00/hour; Gross earnings $225.00. What is the statement actually measuring?

Mika expected the weekend deposit to equal hours multiplied by the hourly rate, but the deposit is smaller. The first move is not to accuse anyone or assume every line is correct. Find the pay-period dates and the hours covered. This classroom pay stub is fictional; its dates, hours, dollar values, and deductions are invented. We are learning how to read and reconcile a statement, not estimating a real student’s tax or benefits.

Slide 2: Calculate the gross amount

Gross pay is before listed deductions. Regular hours 12.5; Hourly rate $18.00; 12.5 × $18.00 = $225.00. Gross earnings = $225.00

Gross earnings are the starting amount before deductions. For this fictional hourly example, multiply 12.5 hours by $18 per hour. The units cancel: hours times dollars per hour gives dollars. Twelve times eighteen is 216, and half an hour at eighteen dollars is nine, so gross pay is $225. Compare that result with the printed gross line. It matches here, but the match cannot establish that the recorded 12.5 hours are the hours Mika actually worked.

Slide 3: Classify the listed lines

Add only the deductions shown as deductions. Income-tax withholding $16.00; CPP line $10.80; EI line $3.60. $16.00 + $10.80 + $3.60 = $30.40

Now read the labels and determine which lines are deducted from this fictional cheque. Add the three listed amounts: sixteen dollars plus ten dollars and eighty cents plus three dollars and sixty cents. The total is thirty dollars and forty cents. In real payroll, eligibility, amounts, employer arrangements, and current rules depend on the situation. These invented figures are not current contribution rates, tax guidance, or evidence that a real deduction should apply.

Slide 4: Reconcile net pay

Subtract the deduction total once. Gross $225.00; Deductions − $30.40; Net $194.60. $225.00 − $30.40 = $194.60

Net pay is gross pay minus the deductions taken from this payment. Subtract the total once: 225 dollars minus 30 dollars and 40 cents equals 194 dollars and 60 cents. The printed net amount matches. Do not subtract each deduction from the previous line and accidentally omit one. Also check whether the document has a different payment method, an adjustment, or an informational employer-paid amount before assuming that the net line equals the bank deposit.

Slide 5: Pause: try the calculation

Use the document, then explain the limit. Gross?; Total deductions?; Net? What is still unknown?. Pause and write your calculation before continuing.

Calculate gross pay and total deductions. What does a match establish—and what does it not prove? Pause to work it out.

Slide 6: Worked answer and next check

Arithmetic can reconcile while a record still needs checking. 12.5 × $18.00 = $225.00 gross; $16.00 + $10.80 + $3.60 = $30.40; $225.00 − $30.40 = $194.60 net. Next check: same dates, actual hours, and applicable records.

The result is 225 dollars gross, 30 dollars and 40 cents in listed deductions, and 194 dollars and 60 cents net. A common misconception is that the deposit amount is gross pay; it is net in this example. Another is that matching arithmetic proves a pay statement is correct. It proves only that these lines add up. For a real discrepancy, compare the same pay dates with time records and the agreement, then ask payroll or check current official guidance. Never use this classroom example as a real deduction rate. Suppose the time record showed 11.5 hours instead of 12.5. At the fictional rate, gross would be 11.5 times 18 dollars, or 207 dollars, which is 18 dollars less than the printed 225. That difference is a question to check against the same dates and actual work record, not proof of intent. A clear follow-up would identify the exact pay period and ask payroll to review the hour entry. The invented deduction lines should not be scaled to estimate a real cheque.

Think about the last item of clothing you bought. For me, it was my pants. So let's look at what factors affected that decision. Was it how you felt when you imagined yourself wearing it? Was it your friends? And what you thought they would think? Was it because you've typically worn this style in the past? Maybe your parents, siblings, or other family members had an influence on your choice. Maybe you were trying to stay current. We've all done it. Did you see a commercial? Maybe an ad or celebrity endorsement that helped convince you? Was it because of a sale or a discount code that you had? Or was it because of your own sense of values, style, and knowing what you really want? In addition to all these factors, it's important to ask yourself when making any purchase, can I afford this before spending the money? Think of there are other things you need you rather spend your money on. Listen, whether it's intentional or unintentional, all of these factors can influence the choices and decisions that you make about spending money. So here's a tip. When you make decisions about spending money, take a moment to think about which factors could be affecting your decision. After all, sometimes we make good decisions like my pants.

FINLIT 101 excerpt, used with permission. The lesson below teaches the idea in text.

Learn

Build the idea

Understand the evidence

A money decision is rarely just “good at math” versus “bad at math.” People make choices within real constraints: money available, time, access, family or community commitments, location, health, advertising, and pressure from other people. A value is something a person considers important, such as connection, independence, creativity, security, or helping others. Values can guide a choice, but they do not dictate one universal answer. Two people can value connection and still choose differently because their circumstances differ. A need is an item or service required for a particular purpose in a particular situation; a want is something desired. The line depends on context: transportation may be essential to reach a remote job, while a particular brand of vehicle is one option among several. Avoid labelling people or their purchases as irresponsible when you do not know the constraints they face.

Required checkpoint

Use Making a Budget — FCAC now

Open Making a Budget — FCAC ↗

Not checked yet

Make the calculation or comparison

Before deciding, separate the offer from the influence around it. An advertisement may emphasize a deadline, popularity, or a discount while leaving out recurring costs, conditions, or alternatives. A friend’s preference is information about what they like, not proof that the product fits Ari. Emotion is also information: excitement may point to a real preference, while urgency may be designed to shorten comparison. A short pause creates room to ask: what job must the purchase do, what options meet that job, what is the full cost, what must wait, and what happens if the plan changes? “Can I afford it?” is not answered by a single balance. It means testing the choice against commitments and a chosen goal, while leaving space for uncertainty. The goal is not to eliminate pleasure; it is to make the trade-off visible and chosen.

Use the result carefully

Use a repeatable decision routine. Name the decision and the purpose; list constraints and known facts; identify at least two plausible options, including waiting or choosing a lower-cost alternative; compare benefits, full costs, risks, and reversibility; choose using the person’s stated priorities; then review what happened. A decision can be reasonable even when an unexpected event changes the result. Reviewing an outcome should ask what information was available at the time and what can be learned, not shame the learner for not predicting everything. FINLIT’s “Factors Influencing Money Decisions” and “Factors Affecting Your Values” materials can prompt learners to notice peers, family, advertising, habits, and personal priorities. Their prompt and video format does not by itself teach comparison, so this lesson adds an explicit fictional case, evidence table, and feedback. Students never need to reveal real purchases, family income, or private beliefs to demonstrate the skill.

Putting together a basic budget can help you manage and control your money. A budget is your personalized month to month plan. It's based on your income and expenses. Now, I get it typing all your expenses into little tiny boxes can seem well...cagey.

FINLIT 101 excerpt, used with permission. The lesson below teaches the idea in text.

Learn

Build the idea

Understand the evidence

A is a plan for matching money coming in with money going out over a named time period. Start by stating whose fictional situation it describes, the dates covered, and whether income is gross or take-home. For decisions about spending, use net income or clearly show the deductions needed to move from gross to net. Convert every amount to the same time unit only when the conversion is valid: weekly, biweekly, twice monthly, and monthly pay are not interchangeable. A cash-flow calendar adds due dates so a student sees when money arrives and when bills must be paid. A budget may include fixed or predictable expenses, variable needs, goals, discretionary choices, and irregular costs. Categories help organize information; they do not decide what a person should value. A plan is a forecast that can be revised when evidence changes.

Required checkpoint

Use Budgeting Tips for Teens now

Find one tip in the PDF that can be applied to a dated cash-flow plan; record the tip and the page where it appears.

Open Budgeting Tips for Teens ↗

Not checked yet

Make the calculation or comparison

Build the first draft in a transparent order. Record take-home income and its timing. List committed costs with due dates, then estimate variable costs using the supplied evidence, then assign money to goals and flexible choices. Add an irregular-cost or buffer line if the scenario allows it. Subtract planned outflows from planned inflows and inspect both the total and the calendar. If there is a shortfall, do not erase it by changing a number without reason. Identify options: change timing, compare a lower-cost alternative, adjust a flexible category, increase income if realistic, seek support, or revise a goal. Some costs are not safely reducible; the lesson should distinguish flexible choices from basic needs and obligations. If money remains, it is not “free” by default; the fictional person can choose a priority for it. If values conflict, explain the trade-off rather than pretending a formula selects the right life.

Use the result carefully

Test the plan with one changed circumstance, such as fewer work hours, a repair, or a shifted bill date. Recalculate only the affected rows, then examine the effect on the goal and on essentials. This is a sensitivity check: it shows which assumptions make the plan fragile. FINLIT’s spending-tracking and budgeting materials explain that tracking can reveal differences between expected and actual spending and that a budget can support goals. For this course, students use a supplied fictional ledger rather than tracking family or personal transactions. Historical video prompts, suggested savings percentages, and examples must not be copied as current expectations. A budget becomes useful when it gives a person more informed choices, not when it is treated as a test of virtue. The evidence of learning is a defensible plan, a correct calculation, and a thoughtful revision when something changes.

Learn

Build the idea

Understand the evidence

A major purchase is not fully compared by its advertised monthly payment. First describe what job the product must do, how long it is needed, and what features are essential. Then identify each cash flow: upfront amount, recurring payment, taxes or fees if supplied, required add-ons, and end-of-term responsibilities. Choose one comparison horizon and apply it to every option. If the continues beyond the horizon, say whether you include the remaining commitment or only costs incurred within the period; do not mix the two. Calculate the total outlay with clear units. For a service or lease, the lowest total may not give the same reliability, ownership, or flexibility. Cost and value are related but not identical: a more expensive option could include a needed service, while a cheap option can be unsuitable if it cannot perform the job.

Required checkpoint

Use Research products before you buy now

Open Research products before you buy ↗

Not checked yet

Make the calculation or comparison

Read conditions as part of the price. A phone, computer, or vehicle offer may include a discount, financing, lease, subscription, warranty, usage limit, return condition, cancellation fee, or final payment. A headline can omit the payment that begins after a promotion ends. Write down what the seller promises, what the buyer must do, and what is unknown. For a lease, distinguish payment for use from ownership; check mileage or condition limits and what happens at the end. For an installment purchase, check total payable, fees, term, and whether missed payments trigger costs. Compare “buy now” and “pay later” carefully: deferred payment moves a decision into the future and may create fees or debt. Do not invent missing terms. If an offer does not state a fee, label it unknown rather than zero. Current market examples must be gathered and dated; the numerical offers in this lesson are fictional for arithmetic only.

Use the result carefully

A fair comparison includes at least one non-price factor tied to the purpose: reliability, accessibility, repair, portability, warranty, or ability to exit. Use a decision table rather than declaring a winner from one line. Calculate total outlay over the same horizon, list conditions and uncertainty, then apply stated priorities. Ask what changes if the person leaves early, the device fails, or the program length changes. FINLIT’s car and lease and phone-plan videos emphasize monthly costs, included features, term, and early-exit conditions. Those are useful things to inspect, but the videos may discuss market or tax details that are date-sensitive or situation-specific. This lesson applies the comparison method to a supplied fictional laptop case; it does not assume today’s price, tax, financing rate, or consumer rule. Students practise asking “what is included?” and “what does the end of the agreement cost?” before making a supported recommendation.

Understand the evidence

Learn

Build the idea

Understand the evidence

Interest is the price charged for using borrowed money, usually expressed as a rate applied to an outstanding balance according to contract rules. A rate is not the same thing as a dollar charge. To make an introductory calculation, the case must state the , annual rate, time fraction, and assumption about the balance. Under a simple-interest approximation with a constant balance, interest = principal × annual rate × fraction of a year. A 12% annual rate is written as 0.12 in the calculation. For $600 held for three months at a fictional 12% simple annual rate: $600 × 0.12 × 3/12 = $18. This is a teaching approximation, not a statement of how any real credit card or loan compounds or bills interest. Real agreements may calculate daily, compound, use different APR disclosures, apply fees, or change the balance with payments and purchases.

Make the calculation or comparison

Keep principal, interest, and fees separate. Principal is what remains to be repaid from the amount borrowed. Interest is the charge for borrowing over time. A fee is another charge specified by the contract. Total repaid is not necessarily just principal plus a single interest calculation if balances change, fees are added, or the rate varies. On revolving credit, new purchases and payments affect the balance; interest can be calculated under specific agreement terms, and grace periods may apply under conditions. Never assume a universal interest-free period or minimum-payment formula. For this course, practice with supplied simplified scenarios where the assumptions are explicit. Before calculating a real product, read the current agreement and official consumer information. When comparing two offers, align the principal and time horizon, include stated fees, show the calculation, and mark missing terms as unknown.

Use the result carefully

Interest makes time matter. If the balance is not repaid, a charge may be applied again to the remaining balance, depending on the product. A simple-interest estimate that keeps the balance constant can understate or overstate the real cost when payments, compounding, or fees differ. The key learning is not memorizing one formula; it is recognizing what information a valid formula needs and checking whether the assumptions fit the document. FINLIT’s borrowing videos explain why someone may borrow and discuss credit-card trade-offs, including the risk that minimum-only payments increase interest and delay repayment. Use those concepts with a transparent worked case and original arithmetic, not copied historic rates or unsecured claims. The next lessons introduce payment schedules and amortization. A learner should be able to say “under these assumptions, the estimated interest is __” and “this is not the contract’s final total unless __.”

Learn

Build the idea

Understand the evidence

An amortizing loan is repaid through scheduled payments that cover the due for a period and reduce . At the start, interest is calculated on the outstanding balance under the agreement’s rate convention. The payment is applied first to interest; the remainder reduces principal. As principal falls, the interest portion usually falls too, so more of a level payment can go toward principal later. A payment is not the same amount of principal reduction. An schedule makes this visible with columns for opening balance, interest, payment, principal reduction, and closing balance. If a payment is too small to cover the interest accruing, the balance can grow instead of shrink; the specific consequence depends on the agreement. This course uses a clearly stated Canadian semi-annual compounding convention for its fixed-rate classroom example. A real contract may have different terms, fees, payment dates, variable-rate rules, or rounding practices; always follow its disclosure and current official explanations.

Required checkpoint

Use Mortgage Calculator — FCAC now

Open Mortgage Calculator — FCAC ↗

Not checked yet

Make the calculation or comparison

To model a fixed-rate loan quoted as a nominal annual rate compounded semi-annually but paid monthly, first convert it to the equivalent monthly rate: i = (1 + j/2)^(2/12) − 1, where j is the annual rate written as a decimal. This conversion is important because simply dividing that nominal rate by 12 would apply a different convention. Given principal P, monthly rate i, and n monthly payments, a level payment can be calculated as payment = P × i / (1 − (1+i)^−n). The formula assumes regular periods, no extra fees, no missed payments, a fixed rate, and payments made as scheduled. On each row, interest = opening balance × i; principal reduction = payment − interest; closing balance = opening balance − principal reduction. Keep internal precision in a calculator and round displayed currency to cents; the final payment may need a small adjustment to clear rounding residue.

Use the result carefully

Longer repayment time usually lowers the scheduled payment for a fixed principal and rate, but it usually increases the total amount of interest because the borrower keeps a balance for more periods. A faster payment plan may cost more each month while reducing total interest, but a payment that strains essential costs can create a different risk. Compare payment affordability and total cost separately. FINLIT’s borrowing clips introduce credit products and the cost of carrying a balance, but none replaces a worked amortization table. Its compounding videos concern savings/investments and should not be copied as loan-payment instructions. Here, the learner follows the monthly balance through a fictional schedule and then changes the term to see the trade-off. Explain the convention and every assumption beside the result. Never present the fictional rate as current, or claim that a simplified calculator reproduces every lender’s mortgage disclosure.

Read the narrated and visual transcript

Slide 1: Why did the balance fall by less?

A payment has two jobs in an amortizing loan. PAYMENT = INTEREST + PRINCIPAL; Interest covers borrowing cost for the period; Principal reduction lowers the balance. The whole payment does not reduce principal.

A fictional statement shows a payment of about 88 dollars and 71 cents, but the balance fell by less than that amount. Where did the rest go? In an amortizing loan, each scheduled payment first covers interest accrued for that period; the remaining amount reduces principal. Because the principal balance changes, the next period’s interest is calculated on a different amount. We will follow the classroom case’s simplified one-thousand-dollar example using a stated Canadian conversion convention.

Slide 2: State the assumptions first

These are classroom figures—not a lender offer. Starting principal $1,000; Nominal annual rate 12%; Semi-annual compounding; monthly payments; 12 payments • no fees or extra payments. Fictional fixed-rate model; full precision internally.

The model assumes a one-thousand-dollar principal, a nominal annual rate of twelve percent compounded semi-annually, and twelve monthly payments. It excludes fees, missed or extra payments, taxes, and changes to the contract. Under the Canadian convention used in this example, convert the stated nominal rate to an equivalent monthly rate: one plus point-twelve divided by two, raised to the power of two-twelfths, minus one. That is approximately 0.00975879, or 0.975879 percent per month. Product documents can use different terms; verify a real contract.

Slide 3: Calculate the level payment

Use the converted monthly rate, not 12% ÷ 12. Principal P = $1,000; Monthly rate i ≈ 0.00975879; n = 12 monthly payments. Payment = P × i ÷ [1 − (1 + i)⁻ⁿ] ≈ $88.71344

For equal payments, the payment formula is principal times the periodic rate divided by one minus one plus the rate raised to negative the number of payments. Substitute one thousand, the equivalent monthly rate, and twelve periods. The calculated payment is about 88 dollars and 71 cents when displayed to cents; we keep the unrounded amount internally for the demonstration. Dividing twelve percent by twelve would use a different convention and would not match the stated semi-annual compounding assumption.

Slide 4: Follow month one and two

Interest uses the opening balance each month. Month 1 opening $1,000.00; Interest $9.75879 → $9.76; Principal ≈ $78.95465 → $78.95; Closing balance ≈ $921.04535 → $921.05. Month 2 interest: $921.04535 × 0.00975879 ≈ $8.99

In month one, interest is one thousand dollars times the monthly rate, about 9 dollars and 76 cents. Subtract that from the unrounded payment of about 88 dollars and 71 cents. Approximately 78 dollars and 95 cents reduces principal, leaving a balance near 921 dollars and 5 cents. For month two, calculate interest from the new unrounded balance, not the original thousand. It is about 8 dollars and 99 cents. The remainder of the payment, about 79 dollars and 73 cents, reduces principal.

Slide 5: Pause: predict the next split

The payment stays level; the balance does not. Opening balance ≈ $921.04535; Monthly rate ≈ 0.00975879; Interest = balance × rate. Pause and estimate month-two interest before continuing.

After month one, the displayed payment is about $88.71 and the balance about $921.05. Estimate month-two interest. Pause and calculate.

Slide 6: Worked answer and misconception

As principal falls, the interest portion usually shrinks. Month 2 interest ≈ $8.99; Principal reduction ≈ $79.73; Balance ≈ $841.32. Same payment − lower interest = more principal reduction.

Using full precision, month-two interest is about 8 dollars and 99 cents. Subtract that from the calculated payment and roughly 79 dollars and 73 cents reduces principal, leaving about 841 dollars and 32 cents. The common mistake is to calculate month-two interest on the original thousand-dollar balance or to say the entire payment reduces principal. The model’s total interest over twelve exact payments is about 64 dollars and 56 cents before cent-rounding adjustments. These numbers depend on the stated convention and assumptions; they are not a current rate or an offer. If comparing this schedule with another loan, keep principal, payment frequency, and assumptions visible. A smaller monthly payment may simply extend the term and increase total interest. Add fees only when the offer states them, and do not compare a weekly payment with a monthly payment by looking at the number alone. The useful question is what the borrower pays in total, when payments are due, and whether the schedule remains affordable. Any real mortgage or loan uses its own contract and calculation terms; this classroom model is for understanding the balance movement.

Learn

Build the idea

Understand the evidence

Debt can grow when and fees are added faster than payments reduce the balance, when new purchases are added, or when income falls and scheduled amounts become hard to meet. Start by organizing evidence: creditor, balance, rate and rate type, minimum due, due date, fees, and whether the balance is still receiving new purchases. Use statements and written agreements, not memory or a social-media claim. Prioritize safety and essential needs such as housing, food, utilities, and transport to work or school; the exact choices depend on the situation. Do not stop paying one obligation based only on a generic classroom rule. Contact the lender through a verified channel and ask about the payment, hardship options, interest, fees, and consequences. Record the date, representative, and terms offered. If a demand feels urgent, threatening, or confusing, pause and get trusted adult or qualified consumer-support help.

Required checkpoint

Open FCAC Module 4: Dealing with Debt ↗

Not checked yet

Make the calculation or comparison

Two common payoff strategies are often called highest-rate-first and smallest-balance-first. Highest-rate-first directs extra money to the debt with the highest interest rate while maintaining required payments on other debts, if the person can safely do that; mathematically it can reduce interest compared with paying extra to a lower-rate balance under comparable terms. Smallest-balance-first targets the smallest balance for an early visible payoff; this can support motivation, but may cost more interest when the smallest balance has a lower rate. Neither strategy creates money or removes contractual duties. Before comparing, check rates, fees, overdue amounts, and whether extra payments have penalties. A consolidation loan can simplify payments or change a rate, but it also creates a new agreement, may extend repayment or add fees, and can leave someone with new borrowing room that increases total debt. Compare full written terms rather than accepting a promise.

Use the result carefully

Scams and high-pressure “debt relief” pitches exploit stress. Warning signs include guaranteed fast results, advance fees, requests for passwords or one-time codes, demands to stop communicating with creditors, and pressure to sign immediately. Do not grant access to accounts or send money because a stranger claims to be an official helper. Verify organizations and current Canadian consumer or insolvency rules using government sources and a trusted adult. This course does not provide individual debt counselling. FINLIT’s credit-card video warns that minimum-only payments can make repayment take longer and cost more, but it does not establish a universal minimum-payment formula or current legal rights. Learners work with entirely fictional balances and practice making a safe next-step plan. The goal is not to shame someone for debt; it is to understand the terms, protect essential needs, and find accurate help before a problem deepens.

Borrowing to invest adds a second risk

Financial leveraging means using borrowed money to increase the size of an investment or purchase. The loan must be repaid even if the asset loses value. In a deliberately simple one-year classroom case, a learner borrows $500, invests the $500, and owes $540 after interest. If the investment rises 10%, it becomes $550 and only $10 remains after repayment before tax or fees. If it falls 10%, it becomes $450 and the learner must find another $90 to repay the lender. Borrowing can enlarge both possible gain and possible loss, while interest is owed regardless of performance. Actual loans may compound, charge fees, require collateral or change rates. Borrowing to gamble or to chase a loss adds an obligation without making an uncertain outcome safe. Never treat a hoped-for return as a repayment plan.

Check the leverage example

If the $500 investment falls to $450 but the learner owes $540, how much must come from elsewhere? The gap is $90. The lender is still owed the full $540 in this simplified case; the investment loss does not cancel the debt.

Compare borrowing with other routes

Read the draft transcript

Visuals: a presenter speaks to the camera. The following case provides the numbers and alternatives to compare.

Getting into debt trouble can be very stressful. Stay on top of your finances. Live within your means and what you can afford. Set your own limits and use debt only when it's to your advantage. Learn

Build the idea

Understand the evidence

Before comparing offers, make sure borrowing solves a real purpose. State what the item must do, when it is needed, how long it will be used, and what would happen if the purchase were delayed. Then compare alternatives that meet the same purpose: borrow from a school, use an existing device, rent, buy refurbished, save, or borrow. Alternatives may have access, reliability, accessibility, or timing limits; they must be checked rather than assumed. A decision matrix can compare suitability, upfront cash, monthly payment, total repayment, term, fees, flexibility, and main uncertainty. The matrix is not a scoring machine that makes a personal choice for the learner. It helps make the reasoning visible so the fictional person can apply their own priorities and constraints.

Make the calculation or comparison

Next test in two ways. First, map the scheduled payments onto a fictional cash-flow plan: due dates, take-home income timing, and committed essentials. Second, stress-test a plausible change such as one missed shift, repair, or delayed reimbursement. A payment can fit an average month but fail when timing changes. Do not call a lender’s approval proof that a borrower can safely repay. For each offer, calculate total stated repayment from payment amount times number of payments, then add stated fees and upfront charges exactly once. If rate, fees, late terms, or total is missing, mark it unknown and request complete written terms. A longer term can lower a scheduled payment and raise . Explain both effects. Current consumer rules and product disclosures require dated authoritative checking.

Use the result carefully

Finally, write a conditional recommendation with evidence: “Given this fictional purpose, time, and constraints, option __ fits best because __. The calculation assumes __. Before proceeding, verify __. If __ changes, I would reconsider.” This form prevents a confident calculation from concealing missing information. FINLIT’s “Why Borrow Money,” “Your Credit Worthiness,” and credit-card materials are useful prompts about purpose, repayment ability, terms, and future income. Their assignments sometimes ask learners to research payday lending or obtain real credit information; this lesson replaces those requirements with fictional offers and a school-loaner alternative. Do not frame borrowing as automatically wise for education or automatically irresponsible for consumption. The student’s job is to compare evidence, not to disclose finances or accept an offer.

Convert a goal into a weekly plan

Before you open Setting Up an Emergency Fund — FCAC: Sam has $35 a week for a jacket, bicycle, and emergency buffer. Which FCAC emergency-fund idea helps explain why the buffer has a different job from a dated purchase goal?

A useful savings goal needs an amount and a time frame. Subtract what is already saved from the target, then divide the remaining amount by the number of weeks left.

Weekly amount = (target − already saved) ÷ weeks remaining

Keep the units visible. A result of $20 means $20 each week, not $20 in total.

A planned cost has a known purpose and date. An emergency buffer is money reserved for an unexpected need, so it should not quietly become the amount used to make an ordinary weekly plan balance.

Learn

Build the idea

Opportunity cost is a forgone option

Choosing one use for scarce time or money means giving up the next best available use. The is not the price tag alone. If Avery spends $60 at a concert, the cost includes the future progress that the same $60 could have made toward another goal. People can value the concert highly; the lesson is to make the trade-off visible.

Required checkpoint

Use Setting savings and investment goals — FCAC now

Find FCAC’s guidance about goal amount and time frame, then connect it to one option on Avery’s decision card.

Open Setting savings and investment goals — FCAC ↗

Not checked yet

Order before optimizing

First protect required expenses and payments. Then compare the timing and consequences of other choices. A short-term safety buffer can prevent expensive borrowing; extra repayment may save interest; a meaningful experience has personal value. There is no universal order for every person, but a sound choice identifies what is lost and why the selected benefit is worth it.

Watch for false precision

A calculator can show the interest saved by an extra payment if its rate and balance assumptions are correct. It cannot measure the value of time with friends or the stress reduction of an emergency buffer. Keep numerical and personal reasons separate in the explanation; do not pretend one cancels the other automatically.

Compare options using the same time frame

Opportunity-cost reasoning improves when choices are compared over the same period and against the same constraints. If a learner spends $60 today, ask what goal contribution would otherwise have happened this week and whether that goal has a fixed due date. Do not compare one evening’s enjoyment with an entire year of hypothetical savings. A choice can be worthwhile if the learner understands the foregone option and accepts its effect on the plan. The goal is deliberate trade-offs, not a rule that every optional purchase is wrong.

Separate dollar effects from personal value

A calculation can show how an extra payment changes interest under stated assumptions, but it cannot assign a universal value to rest, belonging, learning, or time with friends. Read the draft transcript

Visuals: a presenter speaks to the camera. The HTML basket and account comparison below contains the figures used in this lesson.

You need to protect your purchasing power of your savings against the effects of inflation. You see, as prices rise, each dollar is able to buy less. Makes sense right? If the dollars you have saved for the future don't increase in value by at least as much as inflation, the purchasing power of those savings will fall, which pretty much defeats the purpose of saving. Learn

Build the idea

Understand the evidence

describes a general rise in prices across a basket of goods and services over time. It does not mean every price rises by the same amount: a particular item may become cheaper, rise sharply, or stay similar while the overall basket changes. A published inflation measure is a summary for a defined place, time, and basket. It is useful evidence, not a forecast of one household's exact costs. For this lesson, the $100 basket and its later price are invented teaching numbers. They are not a Canadian Consumer Price Index result and should never be quoted as one.

Required checkpoint

Use Inflation Calculator now

Use the calculator’s fixed-basket explanation and dated CPI data to distinguish a higher account balance from greater purchasing power. Keep the lesson’s 1% and 3% figures labelled as a fictional scenario.

Open Inflation Calculator ↗

Not checked yet

Make the calculation or comparison

Keep nominal dollars and separate. A nominal balance is the number displayed in an account. Purchasing power asks what that balance can buy at the relevant prices. If an account balance moves from $100 to $101 while a comparable fictional basket moves from $100 to $103, the balance is nominally up one dollar but the basket now costs more. The ratio $101 ÷ $103 ≈ 0.9806 means the later balance buys about 98.06% of the original basket in this simplified comparison. This is a comparison of the stated basket only; it does not measure a person's full life or prove a particular account is unsuitable.

Use the result carefully

For a plan, inflation is one uncertainty among income, timing, fees, access, and changing goals. Make a useful scenario instead of pretending to know the future: state a current cost, choose a clearly labelled hypothetical price change, calculate the changed target, then ask whether the contribution or timeline still works. Avoid applying an annual percentage repeatedly without explaining compounding and the period. If you consult an official inflation series, record its geography, dates, basket definition, and publication date. Do not use one recent statistic as a guaranteed future rate or treat a broad index as a personal cost-of-living calculator.

Understand the evidence

A resilient response can combine options: increase a contribution only if the budget can support it, extend the timeline, choose a different version of the goal, reduce another cost, or seek current qualified guidance. Each option has a trade-off. A young person should not be told that market investing is the answer to a short-term price change; value can fall precisely when cash is needed. Keep near-term needs and emergency access in view, and compare long-term choices using fees, risk, and time horizon. The FINLIT Investing Money video introduces purchasing power; use only its conceptual segment and stop before its dated generalization about a usual inflation target. The essential learning remains in this explanation and the calculation below.

Learn

Build the idea

Understand the evidence

A financial plan is a connected set of decisions: what matters, when money is needed, what resources are available, what may change, and how the learner will review the plan. Begin with a goal stated in observable terms. “Be financially successful” is too broad to check; “set aside a fictional amount for a training deposit by a stated month” has a target and a time horizon. Goals may conflict. A near-term need can compete with a longer-term goal for the same dollars, so a plan should name the trade-off rather than pretend every goal can be funded at once.

Make the calculation or comparison

Next, distinguish an account from a financial product held in or associated with it. An account is an arrangement for holding or accessing money; a product is an asset or service with features, costs, risk, and terms. The words are not interchangeable. A savings account can provide accessible funds, subject to its terms; an investment can rise or fall and may be unsuitable for a near-term purchase. The name of an account alone does not establish eligibility, tax treatment, protection, fees, or suitability. Verify the current terms with an official provider or qualified source before a real decision.

Use the result carefully

Match each goal to its time horizon and consequences if the value is lower or money is temporarily unavailable. Ask: when is it needed, how certain is the date, what minimum amount is required, what access restrictions or withdrawal costs apply, and can the learner tolerate a loss? A plan can use separate “buckets” for clarity without implying separate real accounts. Keep a contingency for unexpected costs if the scenario permits. Do not use a high projected return to make an infeasible contribution schedule appear workable. Contributions should be checked against fictional income and essential expenses, with the remaining amount visible.

Understand the evidence

A complete plan also tracks assumptions and revision triggers. State whether a return is illustrative, whether fees or inflation are included, and what evidence will be checked again. FINLIT’s planning material usefully prompts learners to connect goals, time, savings, and investments; this course rebuilds those prompts into an original evidence-based plan, omitting dated benefit amounts, historic rates, and unsupported guarantees. The selected video excerpt makes the teaching point that planning still has value when some variables are unknown. Unknowns are a reason to document assumptions and test scenarios, not a reason to claim certainty or give up.

Make the calculation or comparison

Finally, identify when another person or institution should help. A trusted adult or teacher may help a student understand a decision; a financial institution can explain its own product terms; a regulated or qualified professional may be appropriate for complex personal advice. The student should know what question to ask and how to verify the source. Do not request real household balances, account statements, passwords, SINs, or credit reports for a class assignment. Learn

Build the idea

Separate skill from business viability

Being skilled at a task is only one part of earning from it. An employee usually works within an organization’s systems; an entrepreneur also has to find customers, set prices, track costs, arrange safe work, manage records and accept income uncertainty. An initial conversation can ask for criteria or clarification without forcing a learner to decide the legal label alone. Finding the right mobile data plan is tricky. Each different provider offers a number of different packages. You need to know what you want out of your plan and just how much you want to spend. Think about how you use your phone.

Learn

Build the idea

Understand the evidence

Start by defining the service needed: coverage where the person uses it, enough data or minutes for the intended use, and an amount that fits the fictional budget. Do not assume the largest data package is best or that all providers have the same coverage. A plan comparison should use one time horizon and show each cost during each part of the term. If a promotion changes after three months, multiply the promotional price by three and the later price by the remaining months. Add activation, device, roaming, overage, or cancellation charges only when the offer supplies them; mark missing terms unknown. Distinguish a device payment from the service fee. “Bring your own phone” may avoid a device installment but does not tell you the network or coverage quality. This is arithmetic plus reading, not a recommendation to buy a plan.

Required checkpoint

Not checked yet

Make the calculation or comparison

Then inspect what commitment creates. Month-to-month service may allow more flexibility, while a fixed term can have a lower payment or include a device; neither is automatically superior. Record the term, what happens after it ends, what it costs to cancel early, and whether usage beyond the allowance is charged or slowed. Check if the displayed figure includes taxes and fees; if not, label the total as before them. If terms are unavailable, do not calculate a fictional penalty or claim the ad is deceptive. Ask a specific question or consult current official consumer guidance. A contract’s total over 12 months is not always its total over 24 months, so state the horizon in the conclusion. Compare the likely use case against the included service, then test a changed usage case such as less data, more travel, or a move to a different region.

Use the result carefully

A good explanation says, “For this fictional use and this stated period, Plan A costs __ before omitted charges; Plan B costs __; Plan __ better fits the named need because __; this conclusion could change if __.” FINLIT’s smartphone-plan video usefully raises data habits, coverage, roaming, contract length, bundled phones, and early-exit costs. Its specific data ranges, provider landscape, and pricing can become dated. Use the clip to generate questions, then let learners analyse a supplied fictional offer rather than repeat the numbers as current facts. A PDF assignment or quiz can test recall of a video, but the learner needs to calculate from visible plan terms and receive feedback for common errors: multiplying the promotion for all months, forgetting the device payment, or ignoring that “unknown fee” is not zero. Never ask students to share their personal phone bills or account details.

Learn

Build the idea

Understand the evidence

A large decision often combines one-time start-up costs with recurring costs. Start with the purpose and time period: moving for a term, buying a bicycle for a year, or joining a program may create different cost lists. For a move, possible categories include a deposit, first payment, transportation, basic furnishings, utilities, food, communication, laundry, and emergency travel. These are categories to investigate, not a universal checklist or current price guide. Some amounts depend on location, roommates, eligibility, agreement terms, and what the person already owns. Mark each item as known, estimated, or unknown. A refundable amount affects cash needed up front, but may not be a final expense if returned under the agreement; students must still consider when it is tied up and what conditions govern its return. Never confuse a monthly payment with the full cost of a term or a year.

Required checkpoint

Use Making a budget now
