Open Making a budget ↗

Not checked yet

Make the calculation or comparison

Make the arithmetic honest. Add one-time costs separately from monthly totals. Multiply recurring costs by the number of months only if they occur each month and the term is stated. If income arrives on a different schedule, connect the totals to a cash-flow calendar. Then compare total expected cost with the fictional resources available and identify a buffer. An estimate should include its basis and a range or uncertainty note when appropriate. Do not invent a precise utility bill, rental rule, deposit maximum, or transit price. If the scenario leaves a price blank, calculate a partial known total and list what must be researched from dated, local sources. Ask whether a roommate arrangement changes both cost and responsibility; a lower share can also create coordination risks or a joint obligation. A that relies on every uncertain assumption going perfectly is fragile.

Use the result carefully

Run a change test: one roommate leaves, a bus pass cost changes, a move date shifts, or an essential item is unavailable second-hand. Update only the affected assumptions and explain what the person could do next. Options might include delaying the move, comparing a different location, identifying safe school or community supports, changing a flexible purchase, or requesting current information from a landlord or service provider. Avoid telling a student that moving out is an individual financial choice independent of safety, family, disability, or housing access. FINLIT’s moving-out and car-purchase resources encourage consideration of roommates, furnishings, transport, upkeep, and agreement details. The dated prices and generalized advice do not establish what a current Alberta student will pay. This lesson uses a fictional plan and helps students ask better questions; it does not encourage students to move, borrow, or reveal their own family finances.

Making a budget explains what to organize; it does not supply local rent, transit, bicycle, storage, or repair prices. Verify those costs with current local records and quotes.

Learn

Build the idea

Understand the evidence

A stays at the contracted rate for the specified period, subject to the agreement. A can move as its reference rate or contract terms change. Do not assume what happens to the payment when a variable rate changes: some products adjust the payment, some keep it level for a time while changing how quickly principal falls, and contracts may set trigger points or other rules. The agreement determines the result. This distinction matters because “lower starting rate” is not the same as “lower cost over the full term.” If rates rise, payments may increase or repayment may take longer, depending on the product. If rates fall, costs may decrease, but that is not guaranteed. The student should identify whose changes, when a rate can change, what index or notice is used, how often it adjusts, and whether there are caps or penalties. These terms must be sourced from the actual document.

Make the calculation or comparison

For a variable path, use the contract’s rule: if payment recalculates, calculate the new payment using the remaining balance and remaining periods; if payment remains fixed, calculate the changing interest/principal split and whether the balance is still amortizing. Watch and notice

How compounding works

Watch the interest-on-interest explanation. The upward curve is only a simplified illustration, not a forecast; use the lesson’s assumptions and scenarios to test what may change.

Read the draft transcript

Visuals: a simple rising line and large text illustrate interest earned on earlier interest. The chart has no verified data source or forecast; returns can vary or be negative.

But what is it exactly? Basically, it's the snowball effect that happens with money and earning interest, or how interest makes money grow exponentially over time. If you put money into a savings account or investment that earns interest, in the beginning, interest is calculated on the initial amount you started with. But as that money starts to earn interest, you continue to earn interest not only that initial amount, but you begin to earn additional interest on the interest you've already made. And as the total amount of interest earned grows, the more interest you continue to earn. Hence, the snowball effect.

FINLIT 101 excerpt, used with permission. The lesson below teaches the idea in text.

Learn

Build the idea

Understand the evidence

A scenario test asks, “If this specified change occurs, what happens to the plan?” It is not a prediction. Name the baseline, alter one or two variables, recalculate, and explain the consequence. This isolates cause and effect. For example, use fictional market value $500 and compare three one-year outcomes: a 15% loss, no change, or a 6% increase. Applying those percentages gives $425, $500, and $530 before any fees, tax, , contributions, or product rules. These are simple arithmetic illustrations, not expected outcomes or financial advice.

Make the calculation or comparison

The lesson’s simulator separates time horizon from uncertainty. Money required soon may have little time to recover from a decline; money intended for a distant goal can still lose value, and a longer timeline does not eliminate . A scenario is useful when it exposes consequences the student can tolerate or cannot tolerate. Never present the positive case as the normal result or the loss case as impossible. If a product has fees or withdrawals, those terms would need to be added from current verified documentation. Keep the basic calculator transparent so every student can reproduce it without trusting a black box.

Use the result carefully

Test cash flow too. Suppose a fictional learner begins with $200 for a goal and plans to contribute $25 per month for six months. The simple no-growth total is $350. If an $80 unexpected expense is paid from that same goal fund in month two, the remaining amount becomes $120 at that point. Four deposits of $30 add $120, producing a revised balance of $290 and a $60 gap below the original $350 target. The plan must change: amount, timeline, target, or another funding source. State which resource is actually available; do not count the same dollars for two goals.

Understand the evidence

A useful revision has a reason and a check date. If a short-term goal is underfunded, extending the date may be safer than taking more risk, but circumstances vary. If the need is essential and immediate, the student should seek a trusted adult or appropriate support instead of treating a classroom simulation as personal advice. The FINLIT compounding lesson can help students visualize how time and reinvested gains interact, but its later numerical examples must not be used as guaranteed growth or copied uncritically. This lesson uses the conceptual “snowball” segment only, then contrasts it with negative, flat, and positive scenarios.

Make the calculation or comparison

When reviewing a result, ask four questions: (1) What changed? (2) Which total or risk changed because of it? (3) What is the consequence if the original target date stays fixed? (4) What revision best fits the stated priorities? A strong response can say what remains unknown. It should also name the simplifications: no fees, taxes, inflation, contributions, or product-specific rules unless the scenario explicitly includes them. This habit makes a student’s reasoning inspectable and transferable to future information without claiming to forecast markets.

Learn

Build the idea

Understand the evidence

helps people make informed transactions and gives routes for certain unfair practices. Start by recording the specific representation: the headline, price, feature, availability, refund promise, or condition. Then compare it with the overall impression a reasonable consumer could take away and with the final or checkout. A technically true line buried in small print may not undo a prominent false or misleading impression. Pressure tactics, material omissions, bait pricing, and failure to deliver can raise concerns, but a single scenario does not establish a legal violation. Avoid naming conduct unlawful without checking the applicable rule and facts.

Not checked yet

Make the calculation or comparison

For Alberta transactions, the Consumer Protection Act and its rules address unfair practices before, during, and after consumer transactions. Alberta’s consumer guidance gives examples such as misleading claims, pressure, and failing to deliver what was promised. A practical first step for a dispute about a supplier is to contact the business in writing, state the facts and requested resolution, and keep a copy. If unresolved, a consumer may file a complaint with Alberta’s Consumer Investigations Unit (CIU) where appropriate. CIU can investigate potential violations; it does not recover a consumer’s financial loss or mediate a private dispute, and it does not investigate scam texts or calls. Do not imply that submitting a complaint guarantees an outcome.

Use the result carefully

The Competition Bureau deals with deceptive marketing practices under federal competition law, including materially false or misleading representations; it considers the general impression as well as literal wording. It accepts information about such practices but is not the route for an individual refund. A consumer who paid through a card, marketplace, or financial institution may also need to contact that provider about its own dispute process, using official channels. These paths can overlap, but they have different roles. A scam that impersonates an organization and an unfair seller transaction are not automatically the same category. Determine whether there was a real seller/contract, what was promised, whether the transaction was completed, and whether money or account access is at risk.

Understand the evidence

Keep a clean evidence record: screenshot the advertisement and checkout, save the terms in effect on the transaction date, keep receipts and delivery messages, note dates and the seller’s contact details, and write down what resolution was requested. Do not post personal payment information publicly. If the seller’s offer may be a scam, avoid sending more money or identity information until independently checked; report fraud through CAFC guidance when appropriate. For a lawful contract, cancellation rights vary by transaction type and current law. Do not tell students that every purchase has a general cooling-off period or refund right. Verify the specific product, transaction method, jurisdiction, and applicable current guidance.

Make the calculation or comparison

In this course, students identify the exact claim, compare the complete impression with the final amount, distinguish the available reporting routes, and explain what each can and cannot do. All prices and statements in the document are invented. The lesson does not give individualized legal advice or decide a real complaint. Its goal is to help a learner preserve evidence, ask a clear question, and select a competent source rather than relying on a threatening countdown or a social-media opinion.

Learn

Build the idea

Understand the evidence

Begin by separating four kinds of exposure: money/payment route, account credentials, identity or credit information, and tax information. More than one can apply. If money was transferred or a card/payment detail was exposed, promptly contact the financial institution, card issuer, or payment provider through a number or app obtained independently. Ask what immediate security, block, dispute, or recall steps apply and record the time and reference. Do not assume a particular charge will be refunded; institutions review disputes under applicable rules and circumstances. If passwords were exposed, use a trusted device, independently access each affected service, change the password and reused versions, review sessions/recovery details, and enable stronger verification where available.

Required checkpoint

Use Report a Scam or Identity Theft — CRA now

Find CRA’s reporting route and identify the type of scam or identity-theft information it accepts; separate this from the other exposure types in the lesson.

Open Report a Scam or Identity Theft — CRA ↗

Not checked yet

Make the calculation or comparison

If identity details or credit information may be misused, contact affected organizations and consider placing fraud alerts with Equifax and TransUnion using their official channels. Check credit reports through current official guidance for unfamiliar accounts or inquiries. Security-freeze availability and procedures can vary by province or territory, so do not promise an Alberta student that a freeze always exists or works the same way. If a document or device is missing, contact its issuer or service provider promptly. Keep a log of actions, dates, people contacted, and case numbers while storing documents securely.

Use the result carefully

If money was lost or the person is a victim of fraud, CAFC guidance says to contact local police promptly and report to the Canadian Anti-Fraud Centre (CAFC). CAFC reports help create a central repository and support investigations; CAFC is not a refund service. Preserve evidence such as receipts, message copies, sender details, dates, account statements, and police file number. Report an unauthorized card transaction to the issuer promptly and follow its instructions. For a data breach, the federal Financial Consumer Agency of Canada (FCAC) also advises contacting affected businesses, financial institutions, and credit bureaus, and reporting through the National Fraud Reporting System; verify current routes before release.

Understand the evidence

CRA contact needs precise treatment. CRA can call people; never use the false blanket rule “CRA never calls.” If a contact claims to be CRA and the person is unsure, ask for the caller’s name, office, and callback number, end the call, then verify independently through CRA’s official contact-verification tool or contact details found on Canada.ca. For suspected tax-related identity fraud, contact CRA through an independently verified official route. Do not share passwords or one-time codes with an unexpected contact. A caller knowing personal facts or caller ID showing a government number does not prove authenticity.

Make the calculation or comparison

Watch for a second wave: a supposed recovery expert may promise guaranteed reimbursement, demand an upfront fee, request remote access, or ask for more identity details. CAFC warns that scammers impersonate authorities and target people who already lost money; CAFC does not contact people to request payment. Stop, preserve the approach as evidence, and verify through the institution or police already contacted. Be kind to the person affected: prompt, practical action matters more than blame. This is a classroom plan, not a substitute for an institution’s current instructions, legal advice, or emergency response. Students complete the task with a fictional case only.

Quick tip: What Report a Scam or Identity Theft — CRA cannot answer

Report a Scam or Identity Theft — CRA cannot secure a bank account, stop a payment, or reset a password. Contact the affected financial institution and service providers through independently verified channels.
